articles.title_orig: Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court has stayed the execution of Christa Gail Pike, the only woman on the state’s “death row”, US media reported on Wednesday.
Tennessee had been set to execute the first woman in more than 200 years on Wednesday, after the United States Supreme Court rejected a bid to halt it. However, the Sixth Circuit US Court of Appeals intervened at the last minute.
Christa Pike, 50, who was convicted of torturing and killing a classmate when she was 18, was due to die by lethal injection at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, but according to a report by The New York Post, she has asked to be shot by an all-female firing squad instead.
Human rights experts have condemned the decision to continue with the execution at all, but say the Supreme Court can still overturn the stay of execution.
Lawyer Clive Stafford Smith, who has represented many death row inmates in the past, told Al Jazeera: “Very few women are executed, but fewer still in Tennessee – it has been 200 years. So this is a step back to about 1820.
So why does Pike hope to avoid lethal injection in preference for the firing squad, and how does the US put people to death? Here’s what you need to know:
Pike was found guilty of the murder of another young woman she viewed as a romantic rival more than 30 years ago.
In January 1995, Pike, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson lured Colleen Slemmer, 19, into a wooded area and tortured and killed her. All four were students at a Job Corps vocational centre in Knoxville.
The case attracted huge public interest, especially after it was revealed that the attackers had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, which Shipp later admitted to carving. Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull.
Pike and Shipp confessed and were convicted of first-degree murder in 1996. Pike was sentenced to death; Shipp received life with the possibility of parole.
“Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions,” her lawyers wrote.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has spoken in support of the execution.
That she should not be executed at all.
On Wednesday, just hours before Pike’s execution was due to be carried out, a federal appeals court issued an order stating: “The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee determined that it did not have jurisdiction over Christa Pike’s Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(6) motion to reopen the judgment denying habeas relief. Therefore, it is ORDERED that execution of the sentence of death upon the movant is STAYED until further order of this court.”
However, the Supreme Court can still overturn this order, Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera. “The Supreme Court has been overturning stays recently,” he added.
Pike’s legal team previously petitioned the governor to commute her sentence to life without parole. It pointed to evidence that her mother drank heavily during pregnancy, impairing Pike’s brain development and her impulse control.
“The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists,” her lawyers wrote.
She would be the only person to be executed in modern-era Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
Her lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, said scientists now understand far more about adolescent brain development and that her sentence was an outlier.
Stafford Smith said: “Christa was just a teenager, and had undergone horrendous abuse as a child. Now she is 50, a totally different person. It is so pointless – will this really make the world a more civilised place?”
Governor Bill Lee has denied clemency, however. A group of United Nations human rights experts has called for her sentence to be commuted.
The US almost never executes women.
Women account for 18 of the 1,683 people executed since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976 – just more than 1 percent.
Tennessee has executed just 17 people in that time before Wednesday, with Pike the only woman on its death row.
If the execution goes ahead, it will be the state’s first execution of a woman since 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Her legal team and trauma experts say it could force her to relive abuse she suffered in childhood.
Her clemency petition documents childhood violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was aged 11 and 17. It also cites her diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Sexual violence and trauma experts argue that the procedures around lethal injection would likely trigger severe flashbacks of that abuse.
Her legal team also argues that she has small veins and a blood condition that could make it difficult to place an IV line, a claim the state disputes.
In May, Tennessee prison officials abandoned the execution of another prisoner, Tony Carruthers, after failing to find a suitable vein.
According to The New York Post, Pike’s lawyers said she also fears a painful death by lethal injection.
The paper reported that she wants to be shot by an all-female firing squad, with members of Slemmer’s family among the witnesses.
Tennessee is not among the five states that authorise the firing squad.
In court in August, her lawyers proposed hanging instead, noting it was the method Tennessee last used to execute a woman.
The state opposed that, saying Tennessee has neither the equipment nor the legal authority to carry it out. The judge sided with the state but allowed for the possibility of an all-female execution team.
Tennessee also allows prisoners whose crimes predate January 1999 to choose the electric chair; Pike’s crime took place in 1995.
There are 27 states with the death penalty, although four have placed its use on hold.
Lethal injection is authorised in every state with the death penalty; electrocution in nine states; gas in nine; and the firing squad in five. In Idaho, the firing squad became the primary method in July 2026.
Tennessee authorises lethal injection and electrocution. If both are found unconstitutional, its law allows any constitutional method.
Since 2008, the Supreme Court has required prisoners challenging an execution method to identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces the risk of severe pain.
In June, a federal judge permanently barred Alabama from executing Jeffery Lee with nitrogen gas, ruling that it violated the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
She found his proposed alternative, the firing squad, feasible.
The US has used five: lethal injection, electrocution, gas, the firing squad and hanging.
Lethal injection accounts for 1,491 executions since 1976, while electrocution has been used 163 times. Gas has been used 19 times, with Alabama and Louisiana the only states to have used it.
In nitrogen executions, a mask is placed over the prisoner’s face, and the air they breathe is replaced with pure nitrogen.
The firing squad, the method Pike reportedly wants, has been used just six times since 1976.
Hanging, once a primary method, is not currently authorised in any state.
Because none of them reliably work as intended, many experts say.
The Eighth Amendment to the US Constitution bars “cruel and unusual punishments”. But the Supreme Court has made challenges to the death penalty harder to win. It has ruled that proving a method risks severe pain is not enough; prisoners must also identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces that risk.
Lethal injection depends on finding a usable vein. If the drugs go into a muscle instead, or the needle clogs, the prisoner can suffer extreme pain.
In 2017, legal challenges in Arkansas cited botched lethal injections in Oklahoma and Arizona.
Meanwhile, the electric chair does not always kill with the first jolt. If the prisoner’s heart is still beating, another jolt must be applied.

articles.title_orig: Senate Democrats sink 'toothless' stock trading ban, data center bill in last act before election recess
articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats sink 'toothless' stock trading ban, data center bill in last act before election recess
articles.content_orig:
Senate Democrats on Wednesday defeated a pair of bills that aimed to address data center -related affordability concerns and limit Congress members' ability to profit on the stock market while in office, arguing both were watered-down proposals.
The data center bill, dubbed the Ratepayer Protection Act failed on a vote of 57-43. A second bill, known as the Stop Insider Trading Act, which also includes a controversial voter-identification provision, was defeated on a party-line, 53-47 vote. Both bills needed 60 votes to overcome the Senate filibuster.
Republicans will likely use the votes as fodder on the campaign trail this fall, as the GOP seeks to hold  narrow majorities in both chambers despite President Donald Trump 's falling approval ratings and persistent concerns about affordability. The Senate is due to recess as soon as Wednesday, as lawmakers seeking reelection will return to their home states to campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm election .
"EVERY Senate Democrat just joined 94% of House Democrats in voting AGAINST banning congressional stock trading.," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., posted to X immediately following the vote. The bill, he said, provides "the accountability the American people demand. But every Democrat blocked it from becoming law."
The Ratepayer Protection Act , which passed the House on a 417-3 vote earlier this month, would establish a regulatory framework that states could consider adopting to require large artificial intelligence data centers to cover their own energy costs, rather than passing them down to customers.
But Democrats have railed against the measure. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., called the proposal a "toothless messaging bill" in a speech in the Senate on Tuesday.
"The bill is a fraud. I can sum up the shortcomings of Republicans' data center bill with one word: optional," Schumer said.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who has called for a national moratorium on data centers until developers can demonstrate they will cover the full cost of their construction and operation, called the legislation a "silly piece of nonsense."
"Give us something of substance and we'll vote on it," Warren said ahead of the vote.
Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, cited similar concerns when he blocked the bill earlier this month after Sen. Jon Husted , R-Ohio, requested unanimous consent for quick passage.
Husted is in a " toss up " race for re-election against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown . Brown has accused his opponent of helping to bring data centers to the state when he was lieutenant governor.
Husted and other Republicans could use a messaging win on the data center front, which has evolved in recent months into a potent campaign issue as opponents seek stricter guardrails for developers.
Meanwhile, the congressional stock trading bill, passed the House in July on a 232-198 vote, and would prohibit sitting members of Congress from buying individual stocks. But it would not force members to divest their existing portfolios, a sticking point for some Democrats who have advocated a more stringent trading ban.
Republicans also tacked on a controversial voter identification provision to the measure, which Democrats largely oppose.
Schumer similarly criticized the stock trading proposal on Tuesday, calling it a "theatrical farce" and the voter ID provision a "poison pill."
And Sen. Tim Kaine , D-Va., said the Republican proposal was a half measure.
"It's obviously a sign that they don't take seriously the issue of insider trading. If you wanted to get a stock ban done, you would put a stock ban on the floor," Kaine said on Wednesday.
Husted, in a post to X on Tuesday, called both proposals "commonsense, bipartisan bills."
"Lowering energy costs, requiring photo ID to vote, and banning stock trading for members of Congress could be bipartisan wins," Husted wrote. "Senate Democrats are the only ones standing in the way of delivering what the American people have asked us to do."
— Irit Skulnik contributed to this story.

articles.title_orig: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.title_zh: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.content_orig:
Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukraine's Prime Minister has said.
At least five people were killed in overnight attacks across the country, including a child in the Kyiv region, Serhiy Koretskyi said.
The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.
The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. The operator confirmed damage to the plant.
Koretskyi wrote on Telegram: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.
"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."
Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022.
In total, 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there had been strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.
On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.
State-owned grid operator Ukrenergo advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.
Acrid smoke obscured views over Kyiv on Wednesday
In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.
Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.
Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional head Timur Tkachenko said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building.
Another person was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region, acting regional head Heorhiy Reshetilov said.
Two more people were killed in the north-eastern Sumy region on Tuesday, regional head Oleh Hryhorov said. A school was also hit there in a separate strike, he added.
Russia's defence ministry said it had launched massive overnight strikes on Ukrainian facilities.
It said targets included the Trypilska thermal power plant, located some 40km from Kyiv, and claimed the plant supplied electricity to Ukrainian defence facilities.
The operator of the plant, Centrenergo, said it was assessing the scale of the damage.
Russia's military added that it had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions, including Moscow.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said it had struck a number of Russian military targets, including a drone warehouse in the occupied Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine.
Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including a large area of Donetsk.
On the battlefield, Ukraine's Third Army Corps said it had recaptured several settlements near the city of Lyman in Donetsk this week, as part of a counter-offensive called Operation Vivaldi. Zelensky visited troops in the area on Wednesday.
But elsewhere, the front line remains largely stagnant, with both sides failing to make significant gains.

Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.
On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The Guardian has reached out to the state department for comment on whether it had “blown” holds from Congress on releasing the funds due to concerns about their use.
Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).
Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa .
“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”
The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.
“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.
“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”
The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.
In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).
Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.
The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.
“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”
Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the state department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
ProPublica first reported that Trump officials had drawn up at least a dozen no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe and advocates for white South Africans.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.
A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.
A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.
One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.
And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

articles.title_zh: Caleb Flynn, ‘American Idol’ Contestant and Pastor, Convicted of Wife’s Murder
articles.content_orig:
When Alleigha Botner, Caleb Flynn’s 24-year-old then-mistress, took the stand in his murder trial last week, she admitted to several potential crimes she herself may have committed.
She deleted text messages from the night Flynn’s wife was killed. She lied to the FBI to save her reputation. She admitted that she, too, said she wanted Ashley Flynn dead.
But despite her testimony, legal experts say Botner will likely not face any criminal charges. She also said she was not promised anything by the prosecutor in exchange for her testimony, according to NBC News Cincinnati affiliate WLWT .
Flynn, 40, a former music pastor and contestant on “American Idol,” was found guilty Tuesday of murdering his wife in their Ohio home in February and staging the scene to make it look like an intruder committed the crime. It took a jury just over two hours to convict him on nine counts of murder, assault and tampering with evidence in Ashley Flynn’s death.
His trial gained national attention when Botner, who said she and Flynn had been having an affair at the time of Ashley Flynn’s killing, took the stand for the prosecution, testifying against her former paramour. She read from the more than 107,000 text messages they are said to have exchanged during their affair, and the jury heard AI-generated love songs Flynn apparently made for her.
The text messages revealed a young woman who was desperate for her lover to leave his wife, at times even saying she wished Ashley Flynn was dead so Botner could be with Flynn.
Botner said on the stand that she regretted those sentiments, sobbing as she read one particularly painful message: “I want to kill her, Caleb.”
Botner said Flynn replied: “That makes two of us.”
But legal experts told NBC News that the chances Botner is also charged in Ashley Flynn’s death are slim.
“Wanting someone to die or even be murdered isn’t enough for criminal liability,” Neama Rahmani, a former federal prosecutor, said. “Botner would have to be a co-conspirator, accomplice, aider and abettor, or accessory to murder.”
He added: “Unless Botner had the criminal intent to kill Ashley Flynn and agreed to or helped commit the murder, she can’t be prosecuted.”
In at least one other instance, Flynn mused of a life without his wife, writing in one alleged text message from August 2025: “I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail.”
But Botner also told Flynn she didn’t actually want his wife dead. She repeatedly asked him to leave his wife, though, and imagined a future together without her.
“I’m not asking that you take her life obviously, because that’s not what you should do, and I know you actually wouldn’t,” she wrote in another message. “But to make the divorce happen, it would change everything.”
Rahmani noted that Botner’s defense — that she wanted Flynn to leave his wife, not to kill her — is strong enough to avoid criminal charges.
Botner and Flynn continued to message up until the night before the murder. According to the text messages, Flynn told Botner that night that he was “free” and had chosen her, promising they would have a life together.
When she found out the next morning that Ashley Flynn had been shot dead, she texted Flynn asking what had happened, she testified. But when he didn’t respond, she said she deleted the messages because she figured someone would want to look through his phone and she was scared their affair would be found out.
She also admitted that she lied in her first interview with the FBI in an effort to save her reputation, fearful she would be forever attached to this affair — or the murder.
“Destroying the messages and electronic devices after the fact may make her guilty of tampering with evidence or obstruction of justice,” Rahmani said. But prosecutors “rarely charge their star cooperating witnesses after they testify. That would chill cooperation in future cases and is bad policy.”
Mark Godsey, a criminal law professor at the University of Cincinnati College of Law, said there also may be some kind of deal between Botner and prosecutors that will shield her from charges, even if she was not formally given immunity.
“It would be malpractice for her attorney to put her on the stand with zero protections,” Godsey said. “It might be true that ‘promises’ were not made, but in my experience I think there is some sort of understanding that her testimony will help her and get leniency.”
In the four years since their relationship began, Botner told the court that her feelings toward Flynn have changed — and that she now hated him.
When asked why she hated him, Botner said: “Because I believe that he murdered his wife.”
Flynn will be sentenced on Oct. 5. He faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Defense attorney Patrick Mulligan said Flynn will challenge the verdict.

articles.title_zh: Spain, France align on welcoming UK back to EU, strengthening China trade defences
articles.content_orig:
French president, speaking alongside Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez, says EU bid would be good news for UK and Europeans
UK politics live – latest updates
The French president, Emmanuel Macron , has reacted warmly to Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could rejoin the EU.
“Welcome back,” the French leader said in English with a smile at a news conference in Madrid on Wednesday. Macron continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , said his country would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU.
The two leaders were responding to the British prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference in which Burnham said Britain would not have a clear path “until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market” and that Brexit had “done more harm than good”.
In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said the government could maintain the status quo, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” for full EU membership.
Macron said the British had “always been useful in helping us simplify things” when the UK was part of the EU and were “demanding partners”. Burnham “is right to have this boldness”, he added.
Earlier, Macron, who has frequently accused the proponents of Brexit of misleading the public , said Brexit had been “the biggest lie of the last 30 years”, pointing to shortfalls in promised economic growth and trade opportunities.
Sandro Gozi, an Italian Social Democrat, told the Guardian: “Burnham has finally swept away the so-called red lines that have constrained the debate on Britain’s relationship with Europe. That is a welcome and important step.”
The MEP, who co-chairs the EU-UK parliamentary partnership assembly, added: “Europe should respond with the same openness. We should be ready to turn the page and build a new EU-UK partnership, removing unnecessary barriers and restoring much closer economic and political cooperation.”
EU officials welcomed the change in tone but said it was up to the UK to define what it wanted from the future relationship. They have told their British counterparts that the UK is welcome to join the customs union or single market via membership of the European Economic Area .
In recent weeks Brussels has again mooted British membership of the customs union as an answer to the bloc’s Made in Europe policy , which could exclude British clean technology and electric vehicles from valuable European subsidy programmes and public contracts.
But EU officials also stress that joining the customs union would require full alignment with EU trade policy and tariffs. Single market membership means accepting free movement of people, alongside free movement of goods, services and capital.
More than 10 years after the Brexit vote, the EU remains attached to its red lines. A recent proposal from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, that Canada should become the EU’s first-ever associate member , is not seen as a serious option for the UK (or even Canada). The idea is widely regarded by EU insiders as an ill-defined symbolic gesture with no legal basis.
after newsletter promotion
The EU and UK are due to hold a summit in Brussels, with a date in the second half of November expected to be announced in the coming days. The annual gathering was postponed after the resignation of Keir Starmer.
The Burnham government has made resolving Britain’s exclusion from Made in Europe a top priority, but several EU sources say the issue will not be settled at the summit as the EU is yet to agree its internal position on key legislative texts.
France is the staunchest opponent of opening Made in Europe to countries outside the EU, including the UK.
Macron pointed to the limits of the UK seeking close ties with the EU while remaining outside. “You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union, nor can you decide to take what suits you and leave the rest,” he said. “So, come back.”
A European Commission spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union . It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

articles.title_orig: Eli Lilly says closely watched combo obesity regimen boosts weight loss in mid-stage trial
articles.title_zh: Eli Lilly says closely watched combo obesity regimen boosts weight loss in mid-stage trial
articles.content_orig:
Eli Lilly on Wednesday said its experimental combination regimen showed greater weight loss than a high dose of its top-selling drug, tirzepatide, alone in a mid-stage trial on patients with obesity and Type 2 diabetes.
The combo therapy met the study's main goals in a population that typically struggles to lose weight. The results boost hopes that it could serve as an alternative blockbuster treatment option for people who didn't respond to or see the results they wanted on the current GLP-1 products on the market. Lilly said it plans to start Phase 3 trials on the regimen at the end of the year.
The combination treatment combines Lilly's experimental drug eloralintide, which targets amylin – a hormone in the pancreas involved in appetite and satiety – with a low dose of tirzepatide, the active ingredient in its obesity injection Zepbound and its diabetes counterpart Mounjaro.
Tirzepatide targets two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP. Lilly believes that hitting all three pathways, including amylin, can further reduce appetite and improve weight loss – and the combo drug did just that in the 48-week Phase 2 trial.
People taking the highest dose of the combo regimen lost up to 23.3% of their weight, or around 54 pounds, on average. That treatment combined 9 milligrams of the amylin drug and 15 milligrams of tirzepatide.
Meanwhile, patients taking only a 15-milligram dose of tirzepatide saw 14.8% weight loss, or 34.4 pounds, on average. Those who took eloralintide alone lost up to 12.3% of their weight, or 28.6 pounds, on average.
"Patients may not get what they need from a drug like tirzepatide," Ken Custer, president of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health, said in an interview. "They may not get what they need from a drug like a eloralintide on its own. The ability to combine them together and provide even greater weight loss – that's definitely one obvious" benefit of the new regimen.
The combo treatment also lowered a key measure of blood sugar levels – A1C – by up to 2.9% on average. Higher-dose tirzepatide reduced A1C by up to 2.4% on average, while the amylin drug lowered it by up to 1.4% on average.
Lilly may face more questions from investors and the medical community about how well patients tolerate and stay on the highly effective combination therapy.
More patients on the combo regimen – 10.8% to 27%, depending on the dose – discontinued treatment due to side effects compared to the 2.9% of people on tirzepatide alone in the trial.
Up to 10.8% of people on the amylin drug alone discontinued treatment due to side effects, compared to 16.7% with placebo.
Lilly said the side effects were more frequent in groups taking the combination regimen compared to tirzepatide or the amylin drug alone. The most common side effects of the combo therapy were gastrointestinal-related, generally mild or moderate in severity, and mainly occurred when patients increased doses in the trial.
But Custer cautioned against reading too much into the combo regimen's discontinuation rates in Phase 2. He noted that the highest dose of tirzepatide similarly showed elevated rates, around 25%, in a mid-stage trial back in 2018.
"It's probably not the best indicator of the tolerability of a medicine," Custer told CNBC. "We do things in Phase 1 and Phase 2 to test what the molecule can do from an efficacy perspective. We also learn from those studies about how we should administer them, and then we make changes. We do this every time."
Lilly plans to adjust the dosing regimens for the combo treatment in Phase 3 trials, "and we expect that we'll end up with a very favorable balance of efficacy and tolerability," Custer added.
Lilly is also planning to advance a co-formulation of the two drugs in Phase 3 trials, meaning that patients will only need to administer one injection with both tirzepatide and eloralintide.
Results were presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy. On Wednesday, Lilly said it plans to advance the combo product into Phase 3 studies by the end of 2026.
Ahead of the Phase 2 data, some analysts said the study positions Lilly's combination regimen as a direct comparison to Novo's next-generation obesity treatment CagriSema, which combines drugs targeting amylin and GLP-1.
Custer said the combination regimen could "turn out to be a really winning approach."
"This very physiological approach of combining GLP-1, GIP, and amylin, which are three nutrient-stimulated hormones that your body releases naturally in response to food and promotes satiety, putting those things together may just make for a drug that is broadly used," he said. "You're sort of lightly engaging three hormone systems rather than blasting any one of them."
Ahead of Lilly's data, Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger said he sees "mega-blockbuster" sales for Lilly's amylin-targeting drug, eloralintide, which is also being studied as a standalone treatment. He told CNBC the drug likely has "much greater market potential than the Street currently realized," noting that there are "millions" of patients who didn't see results from existing GLP-1 treatments or couldn't tolerate their side effects.
Risinger added that Lilly's combination therapy can also serve as an alternative to the company's other next-generation obesity drug that also targets three other gut hormones. That treatment, retatrutide, targets GLP-1, GIP and another hormone called glucagon, and has shown some of the highest levels of weight loss seen to date in clinical trials.
Wednesday's results reinforce the positive results seen in a Phase 1 trial on the combo amylin-tirzepatide regimen.
In the study, adding a 3-milligram dose of eloralintide to a 5-milligram dose of tirzepatide led to 17% weight loss over 16 weeks in adults with obesity. That compares to 10% weight loss with that same dose of tirzepatide alone, according to Lilly.

articles.title_orig: DA in Cornell University case says he never saw transcript of campus police interview with alleged rape victim
articles.title_zh: DA in Cornell University case says he never saw transcript of campus police interview with alleged rape victim
articles.content_orig:
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten says he never saw a transcript of a conversation between an alleged rape victim and investigators showing what she told Cornell University campus police before his office decided not to bring charges.
The transcript , which CBS News New York exclusively obtained from a source, shows the victim told campus police more than three weeks after the alleged assault,  "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
"I'm going to follow up on this because this is news to me," Van Houten told CBS News New York on Tuesday about the transcript .
Cornell conducted an internal investigation into the alleged fraternity gang rape that occurred Oct. 19-20, 2024, and led to expulsions, suspensions and other sanctions. Criminal charges, however, were not pursued, and prosecutors have now reopened their criminal investigation as the law enforcement response has come under new scrutiny.
Van Houten said his decision not to bring charges was based on the contents of a 2024 statement signed by Jane Doe, the alleged victim.
When Van Houten was told by CBS News New York's Mahsa Saeidi that Jane Doe had said she was confident she was raped, Van Houten said, "That wasn't information that I had, first of all. Second of all, that is a legal conclusion."
"If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more," Van Houten continued. "Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."
The DA said he'd seek the transcript and follow up with Cornell Police.
"Nobody knows this information about the transcript and that gives me something to really dig into because that changes the landscape for me," Van Houten said.
Cornell University said its police department provided the results of the school's investigation to the DA.
Jane Doe's interview, as seen in the transcript, began on Nov. 14 — more than three weeks after the alleged gang rape — and continued the next day. A campus police investigator led the questioning. A Title IX investigator, a victim advocate, and Jane Doe's adviser were also in the room for the first day of the interview.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe described drinking and using drugs the night of the alleged rape, and said she had gaps in her memory.
The transcript shows she distinguished the initial sexual activity from what she says happened later, and when asked whether she was OK with the initial encounter, she said, "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this."
Jane Doe added, according to the transcript, "And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard."
According to the transcript, she said she didn't remember the end of the night "where I was raped" and didn't know how many people had sex with her.
When describing what happened later in the night, the transcript says Jane Doe said, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
The transcript shows that throughout the interview, the investigator asks questions as he prepares her written statement.
Before discussing what Jane Doe said when men asked her for sex, the transcript says the investigator warned her that his questions may sound accusatory, but said he needed specific answers to determine the right charges.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe said she swatted one man's hand away and told him she was uncomfortable, and she told another man no a few times or that she was too tired.
"Was it 'no' or was it, 'eh, I'm tired'?" the investigator asked, according to the transcript.
The transcript says Jane Doe responded, "I think it's 'I'm tired.'"
According to the transcript, the investigator later asked whether she got tired of answering the men's questions asking for sex, and gave in.
"Yes. It was coercion, yes," Jane Doe said, according to the transcript. She also said she was "completely and totally incapacitated."
The transcript shows the investigator documenting her account, reading it back and asking her to clarify or correct it.
On the second day of the interview, Jane Doe reviewed the revised six-page statement. The transcript shows her adviser asked if she wanted her and another adviser to review the statement.
Before signing, the transcript shows Jane Doe said, "I'm very confident about this."
Jane Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, told CBS News, "What more did (Van Houten) need to do a thorough investigation and prosecute? He had a woman who told an officer she was raped and a group chat inviting sexual assaults. The failure to do anything is shocking."
"Neither I nor Ms. Doe have any confidence in DA Houten's ability to handle this investigation and prosecution," Giuffra said. "He seems more interested in protecting his reputation as opposed to seeking justice as is his duty as the District Attorney."
Previously, Giuffra said his client was in denial after the alleged attack.
CBS News New York has not seen Jane Doe's final six-page statement. CBS News New York reached out to Cornell and has not heard back.
CBS News New York is in touch with attorneys for two defendants named in the lawsuit, and they say their clients deny the charges.

articles.title_orig: Will Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Continue Warner Bros.’ Dismal Box Office Year?
articles.title_zh: Will Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Continue Warner Bros.’ Dismal Box Office Year?
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
Tom Cruise has built a career on jumping out of airplanes, scaling skyscrapers and performing other high-wire antics in the name of entertainment. His next stunt may be his riskiest yet: Getting moviegoers to see “ Digger ,” a rare big-budget, star-driven R-rated original comedy.
The Warner Bros. release, which opens on Oct. 2, represents one of the fall season’s biggest gambles. There’s pressure on “Digger” not just to offset the studio’s terrible year at the box office (with bombs including Maggie Gyllenhaal’s punk rock “The Bride!” and DC’s “Supergirl”) but also to impress the new corporate ownership. Paramount Skydance hopes to imminently close its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
It might not be Digger Rockwell to the rescue. “Digger,” directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu and starring an unrecognizable Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon whose company sparks an ecological calamity, is tracking a hugely disappointing launch of $12 million to $15 million in North America. Projections were at $18 million to $20 million but were revised down in recent days.
The film was greenlit at $125 million, but according to four knowledgable sources, the budget climbed to $160 million to $180 million after production went over schedule. A Warner Bros. spokesperson disputes those figures. Regardless, a movie of this size would need a debut near $40 million to justify its budget, per rival execs. Since exhibitors keep about half of ticket sales, and the studio spent another $100 million on marketing, “Digger” has a theatrical break-even point of roughly $350 million globally, according to executives with knowledge of similar films. A Warner Bros. spokesperson pushed back, saying the film’s break-even point is $300 million.
Reviews and word of mouth will factor into the film’s box office longevity, analysts say. They also note that “Digger” could be bigger overseas, where Cruise’s movies tend to make the bulk of their money. Profitability for WB may take longer because Cruise gets first-dollar gross, meaning he earns a percentage of revenues before the studio recoups any costs.
“Kudos to Warner Bros. for taking a chance; Tom Cruise has earned that right,” says analyst Jeff Bock of Exhibitor Relations. “But let’s be honest about where Tom Cruise is today. He’s a franchise machine. Can audiences accept him as a transformative actor again after he’s branded himself as the action hero?”
“Digger” is Cruise’s first original movie since 2017’s hit “American Made.” (That year, he also starred in the notorious flop “The Mummy.”) A bankable draw since the ‘80s, Cruise became synonymous with action stardom through the enduring “Mission: Impossible” franchise and then endeared himself to younger generations with 2022’s blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick.” But even Cruise has learned the hard way that moviegoers have become pickier about what’s worth getting off the couch for. His final two “Mission: Impossible” films — 2023’s “Dead Reckoning” and 2025’s “The Final Reckoning” — faced diminishing returns at the box office.
Cruise, an elusive star who doesn’t talk to press, has worked aggressively — if selectively — to sell “Digger.” Amid his global promotional tour, he made a rare podcast appearance on Travis and Jason Kelce’s “New Heights” and sat for his first cover story in two decades with GQ magazine — which raised eyebrows because the actor managed to avoid any personal questions and relentlessly directed the conversation back to his passion for movies.
“It takes a herculean effort to get word-of-mouth going for a black comedy,” says Bock. “Tom knows he has to go the extra mile with this film. His name alone isn’t going to sell it.”
Beyond Cruise’s star power, Warner Bros. co-chairs Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca were willing to spend big on “Digger” because Iñárritu, too, has a strong commercial track record. His 2015 film “The Revenant” generated $533 million globally and earned Leonardo DiCaprio his long-awaited best actor Oscar. And 2014’s “Birdman” grossed $103 million against an $18 million budget and won best picture. Iñárritu hasn’t released a film theatrically in more than a decade; his last movie, the polarizing drama “Bardo, False Chronicle of a Handful of Truths,” was set at Netflix.
“The combination of an accomplished auteur and a top star has resulted in some very interesting and successful pictures,” says analyst David A. Gross of Franchise Re, citing examples like “One Battle After Another” with DiCaprio and director Paul Thomas Anderson and “F1” with Brad Pitt and director Joseph Kosinski. “But the movie has to connect and satisfy broad tastes. If word-of-mouth is poor, the film is going to struggle.”
Abdy and De Luca, known for their taste and talent relations, faced similar scrutiny ahead of last year’s “One Battle After Another” — another expensive, auteurist swing. That film opened to $22 million and climbed to $213 million globally. Although an impressive result for a nearly three-hour original comedic drama, those returns weren’t enough to get the movie out of the red. “One Battle” lost $100 million theatrically. It did, however, prove valuable in other ways — namely, winning the best picture Oscar.
Moreover, Warner Bros. could withstand the major write-down because it was riding high on a massive year at the box office. The studio had fielded an unprecedented run of profitable hits , including “Sinners,” “A Minecraft Movie,” “Weapons” and “Final Destination: Bloodlines.” In 2025, the company had seven movies that grossed $100 million domestically and commanded 21% of the North American box office.
Fast forward a year, and Warner Bros. isn’t in the same shape. The studio has yet to release a single film that grossed $100 million domestically, and commands just 6% of the domestic market. That’s while the box office is enjoying its biggest year since the onset of COVID , fueled by the best summer season ever recorded.
For all the eyes on Warner Bros. as the studio braces for new leadership, Paramount isn’t having much better a year. Despite profitable releases like “Scary Movie” and “Scream,” Paramount ranks seventh among studios with just 5% of the domestic marketshare.
Warners is expected to rebound with December’s “Dune: Part III.” The third entry in Denis Villeneuve’s sci-fi franchise, starring Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, is shaping up to be the highest-grossing installment in the series.
But before returning to the desert planet of Arrakis, the studio has to mop up a lot of red ink. “The Bride!” will lose $100 million theatrically after collapsing with $24 million worldwide against a $90 million budget. “Supergirl” tapped out with $126 million globally against a $170 million budget, and will lose $80 million. “The End of Oak Street,” a sci-fi adventure starring Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, has grossed $121 million worldwide against an $85 million budget, putting estimated theatrical losses between $25 million and $40 million. “Practical Magic 2,” a legacy sequel that brought back Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock as witchy sisters, is running out of steam with $92 million globally against a $75 million budget; it could lose around $30 million to $40 million in its theatrical run. (A source close to “Practical Magic 2” disputes the loss and says the film could net a $5 million profit.)
Meanwhile the studio’s few 2026 wins were modest: Emerald Fennell and Margot Robbie’s “Wuthering Heights” adaptation, the studio’s highest-grossing release so far with $242 million worldwide, will generate $40 million in profits. “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy” earned $90 million and will yield around $10 million for the studio. “Mortal Kombat II” grossed $129 million against an $80 million budget and will result in gains of $10 million.

articles.title_orig: Braves look to secure Wild Card series win behind Tyler Mahle
articles.title_zh: Braves look to secure Wild Card series win behind Tyler Mahle
articles.content_orig:
The Braves have performed well against Cristopher Sánchez in the past. It could be the deciding factor.
Yesterday afternoon the Atlanta Braves won a roller coaster of a game as the lead changed four times. Ultimately Austin Riley had his redemption arc and hit the go-ahead three run HR off of Jhoan Duran fastball that was in the triple digits in the eighth inning.
Tyler Mahle , the Braves’ best trade deadline pickup will be taking the mound for the Braves against Cristopher Sánchez. Both pitchers were on completely different trajectories to end the season.
Before he joined the Braves, Mahle had a 5.13 ERA in eighteen starts. Since he joined the Braves he has a 1.99 ERA in nine starts, averaging six innings per appearance. In his first eighteen starts, Sánchez had a 2.00 ERA and averaged 6.5 innings per start. Since then, he has a 4.10 ERA while averaging 6.0 innings pitched. If we look at the last month, it is even worse. Sánchez has a 5.12 ERA since the start of September.
This does not mean the Braves will have it easy today. It is a do or die game for the Phillies so if Sánchez starts to struggle, it would not be shocking to see a starter come in on short rest to take over. Sánchez is a very good pitcher, in fact he will likely get some Cy Young down votes. However, on paper the matchup looks good. The players on the Braves’ playoff roster have a combined OPS of .759 against him in their careers.
Ronald Acuña has an OPS of 1.000 in sixteen ABs, Ozzie Albies has a .500 average and 1.193 OPS in eighteen ABs, and Austin Riley has a .467 average and 1.104 OPS in fifteen ABs against him. The rest of the team has mostly struggled, so there is some pressure on these three to perform. Michael Harris, fresh off of a three hit night, has struggled to an OPS of .321 in fifteen ABs.
Mahle has not faced the Phillies nearly as much as Sánchez has faced the Braves. However, he did face them in back-to-back starts in early September. In those combined starts he pitched 13.0 innings and only gave up one run on ten hits. He struck out six to only one walk. He was able to induce a whopping twenty-three ground balls in that span. He did have some luck with a BABIP of .220, but the results were great.
On paper, the Braves have the edge today. It is truly going to depend on if Acuña, Albies, and Riley can continue to rake against Sánchez in a period where he is clearly worn down at the end of a long season. Of course, other players stepping up would be nice too. If Mahle can perform like he did against the Phillies already this month and the Braves can get to the bullpen relatively early, they will be in a good spot. The Braves lead MLB in wRC+ in the ninth inning.
If the Braves win today, technically the Phillies miss October baseball this season.

articles.title_orig: Novak Djokovic: Former world No 1 lands his first win since Wimbledon with victory over Nuno Borges at the China Open
articles.title_zh: Novak Djokovic: Former world No 1 lands his first win since Wimbledon with victory over Nuno Borges at the China Open
articles.content_orig:
Novak Djokovic records his first victory since Wimbledon, extending his record to 30-0 at the China Open in Beijing, which he has won six times; you can watch the WTA/ATP China Open and ATP 1000 Shanghai Masters live on Sky Sports
Wednesday 30 September 2026 14:50, UK
Novak Djokovic returned to action in Beijing 11 years after his last appearance and extended his incredible record to 30 consecutive wins at the China Open on Wednesday.
Djokovic, a six-time winner in the Chinese capital, received a medical timeout in the second set but did enough to defeat Portugal's Nuno Borges 6-3 7-6 (7-2) and reach the second round.
Next up for Djokovic is home favourite Buyunchaokete Bu , who beat Juan Manuel Cerundolo 6-2 5-7 6-4.
"In the second set he started playing better and I struggled a little bit physically to stay fresh," said Djokovic, who arrived in Beijing having suffered opening-round exits at the US Open and at the ATP Masters 1000 event in Cincinnati.
"When I was serving, I was dominating and going through my games quite comfortably. It was helping getting those first serves in, that high percentages makes my life easier in my service games and I played a great tie-break to close it out in two, so I am very happy about that."
Djokovic, 39, was treated on court by the physio at 3-2 down in the second set, but he didn't appear to be hindered by the issue as he saw out his next two service matches to love and played some of his best tennis of the match.
There was only one break of serve during the match, by Djokovic in Borges' first service game.
Djokovic raced ahead in the tie-break and swiftly racked up four match points, but needed only one as Borges found the net.
"That was a really competitive match by the end of it," Annabel Croft told Sky Sports Tennis .
"Djokovic managed to find a way towards that finishing line and actually his service games became more and more efficient. So much of what we talked about in commentary was the physicality of the match and how uncomfortable Djokovic felt."

US Open semi-finalist Karen Khachanov continued his recent domination of Felix Auger-Aliassime 6-3 6-3.

articles.title_orig: Trump Had the Chance to Address U.S.-China AI Safety. He Threw Xi a Party Instead. - Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
articles.title_zh: Trump Had the Chance to Address U.S.-China AI Safety. He Threw Xi a Party Instead. - Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
articles.content_orig:
Trump leading a toast during the state dinner for Xi on September 24, 2026.  (Photo by Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
The summit may be remembered as a fatal blunder, when Washington, Beijing, and the AI industry collectively chose ceremony over action.
The split screen on AI safety last week—between sobering risk and opulent inaction—could hardly have been more stark. In Washington, President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit, rolling out a red carpet at Joint Base Andrews, offering a tour of his ballroom construction site, and holding a ceremonial tea. On substance, by all accounts , the leaders of the world’s AI superpowers said and did little of consequence. Trump did manage to gather a group of AI and tech CEOs at the White House with Xi—not to negotiate AI guardrails, but for a lavish state dinner.
Trump’s AI titans clinked glasses even as their companies released alarming new data about how little apparent control the industry has over its products. OpenAI announced it had paused training of its “ most capable models ” and would resume only with additional safeguards in place after a model “broke out of its secure testing environment as recently as last weekend and took unauthorized actions on the internet,” according to Fortune . Other OpenAI agents had interacted with U.S. government websites, including those of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Census Bureau, in unexpected or concerning ways—just a few of the numerous entities the software improperly targeted. Anthropic, meanwhile, reported that its newest model showed “misaligned behavior” at least 1.5 percent of the time, according to Axios, which reported that AI companies are investigating “tens of thousands of incidents in which the models behaved in unexpected, sometimes troubling ways.”
If the leading AI companies are themselves sounding the alarm, why can’t our national leaders act to avoid a disaster? If a more harmful incident occurs—in the United States, China, or anywhere else—before meaningful action to regulate or restrain this technology is in place, last week’s summitry will be remembered as a fatal blunder, when Trump, Xi, and the industry collectively chose ceremony over action.
With China and the United States racing for global tech superiority, nothing is more important than to keep AI systems under human control, with guardrails to ensure safety. Some kind of U.S.-China understanding, even in parallel , could reduce the risk.
Sadly, that was not Trump’s agenda. On September 22, speaking before the United Nations General Assembly, the president rejected efforts to regulate AI, comparing concerns about AI safety to his other favorite “hoaxes,” including climate change and election interference. “The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” AI, Trump concluded, adding that “we’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.” Following his meetings with Xi, Trump said he wanted to leave AI “exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.” And although Trump’s team put dramatic restrictions around release of Anthropic’s Fable model this summer, those were quickly lifted . Trump’s recent rhetoric suggests no intent to implement anything other than an ad hoc approach to AI safety.
In advance of the summit, Trump’s team did announce an AI dialogue and a new hotline between the United States and China. But Trump and Xi’s meeting yielded no further details or apparent progress. The hotline may simply be an arrangement between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China’s vice premier to pick up their phones in a crisis—the diplomatic equivalent of keeping DMs open—or a more formal effort that, according to WIRED , lacks either approval by Trump or “explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.” While proposals for such a mechanism exist , what we’ve seen so far falls far short of establishing the communication or risk reduction systems that have been used, for example, to prevent nuclear crises.
On its surface, Xi’s position appears reasonable compared to Trump’s. “We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said at the White House. But at the moment, China seems content to signal generic openness to dialogue without pushing any specific approach to improve AI safety. Although two more meetings between Trump and Xi are planned this year, breakthroughs seem unlikely, especially given Trump’s suspicion of AI safety and China’s deep distrust of U.S. intentions.
To the rest of the world, watching the leaders of the two AI superpowers—one authoritarian, the other chaotic and self-absorbed—seemingly content to admire the problem has to be particularly alarming. Rogue AI incidents this summer included hacks of Australia’s Medicare website and a German wiki website , and an attempted hack of a Nigerian cryptocurrency firm . At the UN Security Council last week, the best one UN expert could muster was an appeal to common humanity: “A mother in Shanghai wants her sons to grow up in a world where AI improves their lives, not undermines them. A father in Chicago wants his daughters to thrive because of AI, not to suffer its harms. Our hopes and concerns are the same, in every nation.”
It is not hard to imagine a path that could bolster AI safety at home, address concerning national security risks, make use of U.S.-China diplomacy, and further develop global guardrails—because that is precisely the path the United States had begun to chart just a few years ago.
In 2023 and 2024, former president Joe Biden issued an executive order and a national security memorandum outlining principles around “ safe, secure, and trustworthy ” development of AI systems. The Biden administration also initiated diplomacy with China around AI safety that resulted in agreement that both countries would keep a human in the loop in nuclear command and control. This was a milestone that, while frustratingly limited in scope, would benefit both sides and address a meaningful risk. At the UN, ambassador Linda Thomas-Greenfield shepherded the first General Assembly resolution on principles for AI globally. Although extremely modest, the resolution had the advantage of making the U.S. regulatory approach—rather than China’s—the starting point for future international regulation.
To be sure, Biden-era efforts were far from fully fledged and—judging by the speed with which the industry has developed and risks have increased—arguably not nearly ambitious enough. But that agenda did set a regulatory floor that could have scaled along with the industry. Trump’s decision to dismantle the Biden-era framework immediately upon taking office, along with his rhetoric this week doubling down on that approach, now looks like something even industry itself—and indeed the world—would like to see reversed.

articles.title_orig: UK research funded by China front company being sent to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
articles.title_zh: UK research funded by China front company being sent to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
articles.content_orig:
More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned.
In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state.
Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security.
He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation.
In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms.
This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions.
MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).
"MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says.
"More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.
UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object.
"This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said.
The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated".
It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions."
The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law.
It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so.
Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies."

articles.title_orig: Iran says it got a U.S. response to its peace proposal as its currency hits a new record low seven months into the war
articles.title_zh: Iran says it got a U.S. response to its peace proposal as its currency hits a new record low seven months into the war
articles.content_orig:
Iranian officials indicated Wednesday they have received an official U.S. response to Tehran’s latest proposal to end the seven-month war , which U.S. President Donald Trump had publicly rejected just days earlier.
The officials did not say what the response contained, and whether it was a rejection or not.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the U.S. response to President Masoud Pezeshkian at a Cabinet meeting, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani told the state-run IRNA news agency.
“We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition and will firmly stand up for the rights of the Iranian people,” Pezeshkian said. “The agreement must now be based on a win-win strategy.”
The Cabinet meeting follows Araghchi’s return to Iran after travelling to New York for the U.N. General Assembly last week. While there, officials held indirect talks with U.S. officials and also met with Qatari and Pakistani mediators on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders.
Araghchi briefed the Cabinet on his trip to New York and the meetings he held there, including Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz , which Mohajerani said had been conveyed through mediators.
Araghchi last week said he floated the proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Trump swiftly rejected the proposal , saying Iran wanted to make a deal because it was “losing so badly” but that its offer “would not be acceptable.”
Despite Trump’s public rebuffing, mediators continued working with Iran and the United States on trying to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the strait, according to officials who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration says it is is pushing forward with economic warfare against Tehran as the prospects of the two sides coming to an agreement appears uncertain.
The U.S. Treasury Department unveiled new sanctions on Tuesday targeting people and companies around the globe that it accuses of being financial facilitators or enablers of Iran’s military supply chain.
The latest action by the U.S. administration is part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast” campaign, aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government.
Ten individuals and entities based in Iran, Hong Kong and Pakistan now face sanctions over accusations of procuring weapons and weapon components for Iran’s defense ministry as it fights its now seven-month war against the U.S.
Iran’s economy, which was under heavy strain before the war started, has been in a freefall since the conflict began in late February.
The country’s currency fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging more than 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar in a stark reflection of how the war in the Middle East has steadily eroded the Iranian economy .
The latest decline came just 27 days after the rial hit its previous record low of 2.2 million to the dollar on Sept. 2. The currency has repeatedly reached new lows since the war began in February.
Trump on Tuesday said that Iran is “failing very badly, very badly” and predicted anew that the war will be “over with very, very soon.”
At the onset of the conflict, he had predicted that the war would last just weeks. More recently, Trump said he expects it won’t end until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the U.S.
Also on Wednesday, two men were executed in Iran over their role in violence during nationwide anti-government protests in January, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.
Citing the country’s judiciary, IRNA said the men took part in unrest in the northeastern city of Mashhad that left four members of the security forces dead earlier this year. Their death sentences were upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court before being carried out Wednesday morning.
The unrest began Dec. 28 amid anger over Iran’s collapsing currency and worsening economy and quickly spread across the country, with demonstrators increasingly calling for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic. Iranian authorities responded with a deadly crackdown.
Rights groups say thousands were killed and tens of thousands arrested, while Iranian authorities have reported a substantially lower death toll.

The scandal engulfing Cornell University over a woman’s allegations that she was gang-raped at a fraternity house has caused some prospective students to shun the Ivy League school, college advisers warned.
A former student identified as Jane Doe sued Cornell and seven male fraternity members, alleging that she was drugged and sexually assaulted for hours in October 2024 at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. No arrests have been made in connection to the case, and the local district attorney has said he is reopening the case in light of the civil suit.
Cornell is under fire for its response to the allegations, and Doe has accused the school of failing to protect her or adequately punish those responsible.
Prominent college advisers told the New York Post that several high school students they work with have scrapped plans to apply to Cornell as a result.
“All seven of the college applicants we work with for 2027 who planned to apply Early Decision to Cornell have decided not to apply at all,” Amanda Uhry, the founder of Manhattan Private Schools Advisors, told the newspaper.
“The parents will not permit them to go after what happened,” Uhry said of the seven prospective college students she is advising. “Nobody’s thinking about [applying to] Cornell anymore.”
College consultant Christopher Rim of Command Education said his clients are “shocked” about how Cornell has handled the incident. His international clients are particularly worried and have asked him whether it’s “how all U.S. schools” handle serious allegations.
“Parents who live halfway around the world just want to know their kids are in a safe environment,” he said. “And that remains to be seen.”
At the time of the alleged assault, Doe was 20 years old and a member of a sorority on campus, according to the 101-page complaint filed September 14 in New York County Supreme Court.
The lawsuit alleges that Doe was intoxicated and visiting a friend at the frat house when two male students pressured her into snorting a substance they claimed was ketamine in October 2024.
Multiple male students arrived at the house throughout the night, and Doe was subjected to an hours-long assault by seven of them, according to the complaint.
The filing details graphic abuse including men snorting lines of ketamine off her body, moving her between rooms and continuing to rape and sexually assault her while she was incapacitated.
Doe reported the incident to the Cornell University Police Department three weeks later, and an internal Title IX investigation began in January 2025. However, Doe’s attorney Thomas Giuffra told The Independent that Cornell’s response was severely lacking.
Out of the seven male students named in the civil filing, two were expelled from the university, according to Doe’s legal team. The other students allegedly involved were said to have received lesser punishments, which reportedly included temporary suspensions, required workshops or essay-writing assignments.
Following the uproar over the case, New York prosecutors are reopening the investigation. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office is weighing whether to bring criminal charges related to the incident, but said the allegations in the civil complaint are “dramatically different” from the woman’s statement to police at the time.
Lawmakers and public figures have condemned the alleged perpetrators and the university, including actors Florence Pugh, Mariska Hargitay, Josh Gad and Hudson Williams.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had “serious questions about Cornell’s campus culture and its systems for prevention, reporting, and response” in a statement. New York Attorney General Letitia James is also reviewing the university’s response to the allegations.
Cornell issued a statement supporting the DA’s decision to reopen the case, and pushed back against allegations that the school “did not impose consequential punishments for those involved.”
“A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault,” said Kyle Kimble, Cornell’s vice president for university relations.
Attorneys representing the named fraternity members have vigorously denied the claims in the lawsuit.
